file: Class 13 - More on POTUS - Introducing Procedural Modes Under the Constitution and the APA - 10-14-26.pptx
title: Presidential direction and procedural modes under the Constitution and the APA

topics.heading: Presidential authority and directive power
topics.body: Identify whether the proposed direction rests on Article II, express authorization to supervise, or a statute that places discretion in another officer. The EPA trading system, bilingual education and CDC pamphlet hypotheticals test the unsettled third branch. Presidential involvement leaves the agency subject to its statutory limits.

topics.heading: Executive orders and centralized review
topics.body: The lecture traces a typical order from a lead agency draft through OMB circulation and Justice Department legal review. Executive Order 12866 illustrates a distinct review system for agency rules, including regulatory planning, centralized review and dispute resolution.

topics.heading: Youngstown’s competing readings
topics.body: Jackson’s three positions turn on congressional authorization, silence or opposition. The Venn diagram places Article I alongside Article II to visualize possible overlap. Compare Black’s need for legal authority, Frankfurter’s historical gloss, Clark and Burton’s attention to the tools Congress enacted and declined, and the dissent’s appeal to statutory purposes in an emergency.

topics.heading: Layers of procedural protection
topics.body: Work down from constitutional minima through generally applicable statutes, the organic act and agency regulations. The Fifth Amendment governs federal agencies and the Fourteenth Amendment governs state action. Identifying a protected deprivation and determining the procedure it requires are separate steps.

topics.heading: Individual assessments and general policies
topics.body: Londoner required a meaningful chance to support objections before separately determined paving assessments became final. Bi-Metallic rejected an individual constitutional hearing for a citywide revaluation. Ask whether the decision turned on facts about particular parties or on general premises used to set policy.

topics.heading: Hearing format and APA pathways
topics.body: A hearing can take several forms, including written submissions. The deck maps § 551 definitions to rulemaking under § 553 and formal adjudication under § 554. A statutory on-the-record hearing trigger leads to §§ 556–557. Identify the trigger and any independent sources of procedure for the particular agency action.

conflicts.heading: Noel Canning’s short-recess presumption
conflicts.body: The recap uses a categorical ten-day shorthand. Noel Canning held that a recess of three days or fewer is too short and treated a recess of more than three but fewer than ten days as presumptively too short, allowing for highly unusual circumstances. The Senate also must retain the capacity to transact business for a declared session to count.

conflicts.heading: Informal adjudication still has APA protections
conflicts.body: The matrix describes informal adjudication as outside the APA. It falls outside the APA’s formal hearing provisions. Generally applicable provisions such as §§ 555 and 558 can still apply, alongside the organic statute, agency rules and due process.

conflicts.heading: Section 553(c) and formal rulemaking
conflicts.body: The matrix’s transition from § 553 to §§ 556–557 refers to the route into the formal proceedings. Sections 556–557 replace § 553(c) where triggered. Check any applicable § 553 provisions outside subsection (c) and any additional procedure supplied by the organic statute.

file: Class 14 - Delegating Adjudicative Power - Procedural Due Process  - 10-19- 2026.pptx
title: Delegating adjudicative power and procedural due process

topics.heading: Rulemaking and adjudication under § 551
topics.body: Use the APA’s defined outputs. Rules may have particular applicability and a future effect. Adjudication is the process for producing an order, which can have broader precedential effects. The deck tests the distinction with an FTC complaint affecting other firms, FCC captioning standards for five networks and a loan fee applying across a program.

topics.heading: Ratemaking and licensing cross the intuitive categories
topics.body: The deck’s table separates the statutory classification from the function’s mixed features. The APA treats ratemaking as rulemaking and licensing as adjudication even though licenses authorize future activity and rates can draw on judgments about past costs or practices.

topics.heading: Potential constitutional bases for agency adjudication
topics.body: Start with the nature of the claim. The lecture uses Murray’s Lessee to introduce public rights and describes adjunct fact-finding, integration into a federal regulatory scheme and consent as other historically relevant routes. The slide asking whether court removal might cure a problem is a hypothetical.

topics.heading: Jarkesy’s two questions
topics.body: First ask whether the statutory claim is legal in nature, giving particular weight to the remedy. Then ask whether the public-rights exception permits agency adjudication. Jarkesy involved a fraud analogue and civil penalties serving punishment and deterrence. Atlas Roofing involved statutory obligations without a common-law analogue. The dissent would have allowed adjudication of the government’s statutory enforcement claim.

topics.heading: Liberty, property and the changing public sector
topics.body: The lecture uses Reich’s New Property and Cafeteria Workers to contrast the economic importance of a benefit with the legal basis for claiming it. Cafeteria Workers involved exclusion from a specific military installation, with the employee’s occupation otherwise open to her. Identify the precise interest and effect of the deprivation.

topics.heading: Discretion-limiting terms and the scholarship hypothetical
topics.body: Roth and Perry v. Sindermann distinguish an expectation from an entitlement grounded in an independent source such as a statute, rule or mutually explicit understanding. Compare the scholarship promised after a stated GPA with one that officials may award based on an evaluative judgment. Identify the criteria the claimant can invoke, then use Mathews to decide the procedure.

conflicts.heading: The APA’s formal-adjudication threshold
conflicts.body: The recap’s shorthand about APA coverage concerns §§ 554 and 556–557. The Atlas casebook account also identifies generally applicable APA provisions for informal adjudication.

conflicts.heading: The scope of the due-process requirement
conflicts.body: The deck’s heading about due process and Congress addresses the Londoner–Bi-Metallic individual-hearing distinction. An adjudicative deprivation can require individual process. Congress can impose statutory safeguards on rulemaking and remains subject to independent constitutional constraints.

title: Mathews balancing and statutory hearing rights

topics.heading: The three steps of a due-process analysis
topics.body: Classify the government action under Londoner and Bi-Metallic. Identify the protected deprivation, grounding a claimed property interest in the discretion-limiting law the claimant can invoke. Then apply Mathews to the specific missing safeguard and the time at which it could help.

topics.heading: What extra procedure buys in Mathews
topics.body: Weigh the private interest, error risk and marginal value of another safeguard, and the government’s functional and fiscal interests. The deck contrasts expert assessment of written medical evidence with the claimant’s hardship, and asks who bears uncertainty about whether added procedure improves results.

topics.heading: Loudermill and the timing of a meaningful response
topics.body: The lecture applies Mathews to for-cause public employment. Notice of the charges, an explanation of the employer’s evidence and a chance to respond come before removal, in light of the fuller review available afterward. The apparent clarity of the underlying fact still leaves room to contest significance, intent or appropriate discipline.

topics.heading: Access to evidence and cross-examination are separate safeguards
topics.body: Use the Brock voting table to analyze disclosure of the adverse evidence and cross-examination separately. The controlling middle position required information about the evidence and an opportunity to respond at the preliminary reinstatement stage while allowing cross-examination to await later process.

topics.heading: Three ways statutes lead to a hearing
topics.body: A statute can create a property interest protected by constitutional due process, trigger APA on-the-record procedures, or provide its own form of hearing. The table and hearing images distinguish a legislative-style opportunity to present views from a trial-type process for testing disputed evidence.

topics.heading: Florida East Coast’s construction of the hearing requirement
topics.body: Read the Interstate Commerce Act with the APA. The prospective freight-car proceeding and the 1966 amendment’s substantive factors did not establish an APA on-the-record requirement. The statute’s own hearing requirement allowed written participation on these facts. The deck asks, separately, whether written evidence could also suffice in a proceeding where § 556(d) did apply.

topics.heading: Marathon Oil and the nature of the proceeding
topics.body: The Ninth Circuit treated individual effluent-discharge permits as adjudication and inferred the formal record requirement from the statute’s hearing language and the type of proceeding. Material omitted from the certified record required a remand. The lecture presents this as a contrast with Florida East Coast and flags the division of approaches outside the Ninth Circuit.

topics.heading: Third-party participation and comparative hearings
topics.body: The organic statute or agency rules can permit third parties to seek or join agency hearings. In Ashbacker, granting one of two simultaneous bona fide mutually exclusive applications first would defeat the loser’s statutory hearing. Comparative consideration makes the promised participation meaningful.

conflicts.heading: Loudermill appears in the assigned casebook pages
conflicts.body: The deck labels Loudermill unassigned and marks the full-opinion quotation as outside the casebook. Mashaw p. 487, within the Class 14 assignment, discusses and quotes Loudermill. Retain the distinction between a casebook note, a standalone assigned opinion and the fuller Class 15 lecture treatment.

conflicts.heading: Mathews does not prescribe a universal formal hearing
conflicts.body: The checklist compresses common safeguards and suggests a full hearing for any substantial interest. The governing inquiry is context-specific. Existing procedures, the timing and nature of any later opportunity, and the marginal benefit of a trial-type hearing determine what due process requires.

file: Class 16 - Agency RM and Choice of Procedure 10-26-2026.pptx
title: Agency rulemaking and choice of procedure

topics.heading: Two distinct issues in Marathon Oil
topics.body: The APA record requirement barred reliance on the internal report that never entered the certified record. The regional director could decide this initial licensing matter despite objections based on the agency’s separation of functions and alleged bias. Identify the specific licensing exception and keep the statutory and constitutional objections distinct.

topics.heading: Informal adjudication and hybrid rulemaking
topics.body: Agencies can resolve initial applications, inspections and investigations through informal adjudication, sometimes with tailored procedures and later review. Hybrid rulemaking adds requirements such as a docket or legislative-style hearing to notice and comment. These proceedings can conduct meaningful participation without importing the complete formal hearing framework.

topics.heading: Notice, settlement and separation of functions
topics.body: Sections 554 and 556 address notice, opportunities to settle and who may preside. The classroom ex parte table compares § 554(d)’s safeguard against private consultation on facts in issue with § 557(d)’s bar on relevant merits communications between interested outsiders and decisional personnel. Check the applicable exceptions and scope before applying either provision.

topics.heading: Official notice and the record
topics.body: An agency’s official notice can reach material beyond the usual judicial-notice categories. Section 556(e) protects the party’s opportunity, on timely request, to show the contrary when a noticed material fact outside the evidence supports the decision.

topics.heading: Reliable hearsay under Perales
topics.body: Written reports from examining physicians could constitute substantial evidence in the circumstances of Perales. Distinguish the reports’ reliability and the opportunity to subpoena their authors from the separate question whether a state requires some nonhearsay support under a residuum rule.

topics.heading: The separate stages of § 553
topics.body: Identify proposal notice, public comment, the statement of basis and purpose and the final rule’s effective-date interval. The classroom table distinguishes exclusions from all of § 553, exemptions affecting proposal notice and related comment and exemptions from the 30-day effective-date requirement. A good-cause finding is tied to the requirement the agency seeks to skip.

topics.heading: Same policy issue, different legal instruments
topics.body: The airline stock-sale problem asks whether the second instrument explains an existing transfer restriction or supplies a new operative obligation. The FTC examples compare a binding standard for deceptive advertising, an interpretation of an existing standard, discretionary enforcement guidance and individual adjudications applying the standard.

conflicts.heading: Substantial-evidence review depends on the review provision
conflicts.body: Slide 12’s broad formulation is useful for the hearsay example. In a federal APA problem, § 706(2)(E) applies to proceedings under §§ 556–557 or otherwise reviewed on a statutorily provided hearing record. Identify any applicable organic-statute or state-law review standard separately.

conflicts.heading: Interpretive rules and their underlying law
conflicts.body: The slide calls interpretations binding in a limited sense. The existing statute or legislative rule supplies the binding duty. An interpretive rule can state an agency view of that duty. It needs the corresponding legislative-rule authority and procedures if it imposes a new binding obligation.

file: Class 17 - Choice of Procedure - Notice and Comment - 10-28-2026.pptx
title: Choice of procedure and notice and comment

topics.heading: Policy instruments and the participation tradeoff
topics.body: Compare the slide matrix across three routes. Notice and comment brings wider participation and a record of competing views. An interpretive rule can convey the agency’s view quickly but usually has a thinner testing record. Adjudication develops policy through individual disputes, with formal safeguards for the targeted party where applicable.

topics.heading: Chenery I and II answer different questions
topics.body: Chenery I rejected the SEC’s stated equity-precedent rationale and required the agency to reconsider. Chenery II allowed the SEC to explain the outcome through its statutory policy judgment and develop the principle in adjudication. Compare agency authority to use both modes, the reasons actually given and fairness when imposing an unfamiliar norm.

topics.heading: Rules can resolve general premises of an individual case
topics.body: Heckler v. Campbell, identified as a supplemental case, illustrates the allocation. The Social Security grid resolves recurring vocational questions using categories such as age, education and prior work. The claimant still receives a meaningful hearing on individual characteristics and whether the grid applies to those facts.

topics.heading: Changing an existing rule
topics.body: The APA’s definition of rulemaking includes amending or repealing a rule. Identify the binding existing rule and the procedure needed to amend it. The lecture distinguishes formally changing a rule from deciding an individual case under it, with separate considerations for internal practice rules.

topics.heading: FTC rulemaking authority and noncompetes
topics.body: Petroleum Refiners read §§ 5 and 6(g) of the FTC Act together and treated rulemaking as complementing case-by-case enforcement. The lecture tests a different application in the FTC’s 2024 competition rule, separating the claimed source of competition-rule authority from special statutory procedures for unfair or deceptive practices.

topics.heading: Nova Scotia’s notice and technical record
topics.body: The chart compares the FDA’s original time-temperature-salinity proposal with the final brining alternative and the rejected species-specific approach. The federal enforcement proceeding exposed the scientific studies behind the rule. The Second Circuit held that failing to disclose the relied-on technical basis prevented meaningful participation.

topics.heading: The statement of basis and purpose addresses material objections
topics.body: Nova Scotia identifies unanswered questions about applying one standard across fish species, the suggested lower-temperature alternatives and whether the rule would make whitefish commercially infeasible. A concise explanation still needs to show how the agency addressed significant objections bearing on the adopted rule.

conflicts.heading: Noncompete litigation posture
conflicts.body: Slide 23 compresses two proceedings. The Northern District of Texas set the rule aside in Ryan. The Middle District of Florida granted preliminary relief in Properties of the Villages. In September 2025 the FTC moved to end both appeals and acceded to the Texas vacatur. These were district-court dispositions followed by dismissed appeals.

conflicts.heading: The FTC Act specifies an informal hearing opportunity
conflicts.body: The slide’s shorthand for 15 U.S.C. § 57a refers to the statutory opportunity for an informal hearing and certain procedures for disputed material facts. The unfair-or-deceptive-practices statute does not invoke the ordinary APA formal hearing procedure under §§ 556–557.

conflicts.heading: Public availability alone does not answer Nova Scotia
conflicts.body: The slide lists publicly available data and expertise as possible reasons disclosure might be unnecessary. The opinion held that the agency had to identify the research on which it relied even though pertinent research was readily available. The court recognized that an agency can draw on its own expertise outside the record, but the public still needs enough information about the decisive scientific basis to comment effectively.

file: Class 18 - From Vermont Yankee to Hard Look Review - 11-2-2026.pptx
title: From Vermont Yankee to Hard Look Review

topics.heading: A final rule needs fair notice
topics.body: The logical-outgrowth inquiry asks whether the proposal gave interested people a fair chance to address the approach adopted. Mock contrasts ATF’s proposed point system with its final balancing test. The dissent treated some actual comments as evidence of notice.

topics.heading: Participation depends on usable information
topics.body: Online dockets, advance notices and meetings can make rulemaking more accessible. The class asks who can make informed comments and how agencies can respond effectively when the volume of submissions rises.

topics.heading: Vermont Yankee limits judicial additions to procedure
topics.body: The disputed nuclear-fuel rule used an environmental-impact table. The lecture separates whether the evidence could support the rule from whether a court could require cross-examination beyond the governing procedural law.

topics.heading: Informal proceedings still need a reviewable account
topics.body: The lecture asks whether undisclosed contacts can impair review of rulemaking. It also contrasts the different prejudgment standards used in adjudication and rulemaking and connects meaningful notice with the agency’s final explanation.

topics.heading: Boyd distinguishes an informal record from a formal hearing
topics.body: The Safety Act’s reference to APA procedures and a record for review did not require a trial-type hearing for the factory-installed head-restraint rule. Statutory language, legislative history and the legislative nature of the task all informed the reading.

topics.heading: The basis-and-purpose statement must explain major choices
topics.body: Boyd reads § 553(c) to require enough explanation to identify significant issues and understand the agency’s resolution. A short statement can suffice when the explanation and record show the agency’s reasoning.

topics.heading: Brinegar tests an agency’s evidence against statutory criteria
topics.body: The tire-marking exercise tests the safety benefit and practicability of agency-added labels. The court had to distinguish the lack of factual support for practicability from the agency’s inadequate response to retreaders’ objections.

conflicts.heading: Boyd involved the 1966 Safety Act
conflicts.body: Slide 24 dates the Act to 1968. The Atlas brief correctly dates the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act to 1966 and the Boyd opinion to 1968.

authority.label: National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act of 1966

file: Class 19 - Hard Look Review and  553 Exceptions 2- 11-4- 2026.pptx
title: Hard Look Review and § 553 Exceptions

topics.heading: State Farm requires reasons within a narrow scope of review
topics.body: Identify the agency’s own explanation and test it against the record and the criteria Congress supplied. A court may discern an imperfectly stated rationale, but it cannot supply a discretionary judgment the agency never made.

topics.heading: Rescinding a rule requires considering obvious alternatives
topics.body: The passive-restraint rescission omitted an airbag-only option. The Justices also disagreed about whether the agency adequately explained its prediction that drivers would disconnect automatic belts.

topics.heading: Predictive judgments need a reasoned record
topics.body: The diesel-emissions rule turned on development steps and the likelihood of completing them by the compliance deadline. The court assessed whether the agency answered serious objections and explained its forecast.

topics.heading: Vacatur and remand are distinct remedial choices
topics.body: The course compares remand with and without vacatur and asks whether leaving a rule temporarily in effect could undermine prompt correction.

topics.heading: Match a § 553 exception to the duty at issue
topics.body: The lecture distinguishes exemptions from the whole section, exemptions affecting notice and public procedure, and exemptions from advance publication. A claim of good cause must identify the specific statutory ground.

topics.heading: A policy statement leaves room for decision
topics.body: Compare how the agency uses the document with how it labels it. Community Nutrition and General Electric ask whether purported guidance binds field staff, applicants or the decision-maker in practice.

topics.heading: Guidance classification can shape reviewability
topics.body: A claim that guidance effectively establishes a binding rule can raise both notice-and-comment and finality issues. The DAPA example asks what evidence shows that officials actually retain case-by-case discretion.

conflicts.heading: APA § 704 has two routes to review
conflicts.body: Slide 24 describes APA review as available only for final agency action. Section 704 also covers agency action expressly made reviewable by statute. An agency’s policy label does not itself settle the § 704 question.

file: Class 20 - Review under the Arbitrary and Capricious Standard 11-9-26 - 2026.pptx
title: Review under the Arbitrary and Capricious Standard

topics.heading: Locate the existing legal obligation
topics.body: An interpretive rule explains a pre-existing obligation. American Mining Congress asks whether existing law would support enforcement without the new statement, whether the agency invoked legislative authority and whether the statement effectively amended a legislative rule.

topics.heading: An implementation choice can create new law
topics.body: Compare the accessible-sightline examples with Hoctor’s eight-foot fence rule. The closer an instruction follows from existing language, the stronger its claim to be interpretive. A specific requirement chosen among several permissible alternatives can require legislative-rule procedures.

topics.heading: Changing a genuine interpretation and imposing a new rule
topics.body: Perez allows an agency to revise a genuine interpretive rule without notice and comment. The adoption guidance case illustrates the different issue of adding categorical restrictions without a sufficient basis in existing law.

topics.heading: Good cause and alternative publication sequences
topics.body: An agency invoking good cause must explain it when issuing the rule. Direct final and interim final procedures can still invite comments. Little Sisters asks whether an interim notice provided the information and opportunity the APA requires.

topics.heading: Overton Park starts with reviewability and statutory authority
topics.body: Ask first whether governing law supplies a judicial standard and then how that law limits the agency. The parkland statute constrained the Secretary’s assessment of a feasible and prudent alternative more than an open-ended balancing test would.

topics.heading: Review the agency’s actual rationale
topics.body: The class tests the line between explaining a contemporaneous rationale and inventing a new justification in court. Department of Commerce illustrates remand when the stated reason turns out to be pretextual.

conflicts.heading: Substantial evidence can apply under a special review statute
conflicts.body: Slide 28 limits APA § 706(2)(E) to §§ 556–557 proceedings. The provision also applies where an action is otherwise reviewed on the statutory record of an agency hearing.

file: Class 21 - Reviewing Findings of Fact and Interpretations of Law Before Chevron 11-11-2026.pptx
title: Reviewing Findings of Fact and Interpretations of Law Before Chevron

topics.heading: Pacifica left room for later policy disputes
topics.body: Earlier FCC treatment of isolated expletives and the move toward context-sensitive enforcement frame the policy-change question in Fox. Pacifica’s limited holding did not settle every later use or a criminal application.

topics.heading: Fox tests reasons for changing policy
topics.body: The agency must acknowledge the change and give good reasons. Prior factual findings and serious reliance can demand more explanation. The lecture contrasts the Court’s test with Kennedy’s concurrence and Breyer’s dissent.

topics.heading: Regents separates alternatives, reliance and later rationales
topics.body: DHS needed to consider preserving deferred action without associated benefits and to assess serious reliance interests. A later memorandum supplying a new rationale did not cure those omissions.

topics.heading: Substantial evidence means looking at the whole record
topics.body: Universal Camera requires consideration of evidence that cuts against the agency, including the examiner’s credibility assessment. Allentown tests whether the agency’s announced standard was actually applied to the evidence.

topics.heading: ADAPSO distinguishes the available record
topics.body: The D.C. Circuit treated the minimum evidentiary support required for factual findings as equivalent under the two review standards. It distinguished the formal record from other material that was before the agency when it acted.

topics.heading: Mixed questions combine law, fact and application
topics.body: Hearst asks whether the agency may treat news sellers as employees, whether the findings are supported and whether applying the category reasonably serves the statute. The hypothetical makes the distinct inquiries visible.

topics.heading: Skidmore respect comes from persuasive reasoning
topics.body: In the firefighters’ waiting-time case, the agency’s legal position furnished potentially useful guidance. Its thoroughness, reasoning and consistency determined the weight it earned.

topics.heading: The historical Chevron inquiry asked two different questions
topics.body: The stationary-source example separates an independently resolved question at step one from a permissible agency construction at step two. The class compares modest and expansive accounts of how much Chevron changed earlier practice.

conflicts.heading: Regents was a 2020 DHS case
conflicts.body: Slide 16 dates the case to 2015 and refers to HHS. The Supreme Court decided Regents in 2020. The agency was the Department of Homeland Security. The 2015 date belongs to the separate DAPA appellate decision cited in the lecture.

conflicts.heading: The Fox standard was part of the Court’s opinion
conflicts.body: Slides 10 and 11 call the relevant reasoning a plurality. Scalia wrote for the Court on the ordinary policy-change standard and its principal application. Only Part III-E lacked a majority.

title: The Post-Chevron Era

topics.heading: Chevron and hard look review addressed different questions
topics.body: The lecture reviews Chevron’s historical two steps and arguments for and against deference, then separately identifies why a policy choice or factual judgment can fail reasoned-decisionmaking review.

topics.heading: Mead’s historical threshold asked about force of law
topics.body: Chevron eligibility turned on whether Congress delegated force-of-law authority and whether the agency acted through it. The customs letters applied to particular transactions and were issued in great numbers without ordinary public procedure.

topics.heading: Skidmore asks what makes an interpretation persuasive
topics.body: The lecture tests thoroughness, quality of reasoning, consistency, expertise and the nature of public input. The agency can earn weight even when the form of its interpretation does not qualify for historical Chevron treatment.

topics.heading: King illustrates an extraordinary issue under Chevron
topics.body: The Court independently decided whether ACA tax credits reached federal exchanges because of the issue’s significance, its centrality to the scheme and the mismatch with IRS expertise. The class compares possible applications to other agency disputes.

topics.heading: Apply Loper Bright to the question actually presented
topics.body: The fisheries statute permits observer requirements and expressly allocates costs for some groups. The dispute concerned whether other vessel owners could be required to pay. The Supreme Court set the standard of review and remanded the observer-payment cases.

topics.heading: Independent judgment preserves actual delegated choices
topics.body: Courts independently identify the best statutory reading and the boundaries of any delegation. Within those bounds the agency exercises the delegated discretion and supplies a reasoned explanation. Statutory ambiguity alone no longer triggers Chevron.

topics.heading: Prior statutory holdings and historical interpretations
topics.body: The Court distinguished rejecting Chevron’s method from reopening holdings on particular agency actions. The lecture compares majority and dissent accounts of earlier practice, workability and reliance.

title: Evidence of commercial context

topics.heading: Commercial context and a final writing
topics.body: Use UCC §§ 1-303(d)–(e) and 2-202 together. Commercial context can explain or supplement a final writing and can qualify its terms. Reconcile the sources whenever reasonable. If they conflict, express terms take priority, then course of performance, course of dealing, and usage of trade.

topics.heading: Identify the source of the practice
topics.body: Course of performance concerns repeated occasions under the disputed transaction and the other party’s knowing acceptance or acquiescence. Course of dealing concerns prior transactions between the parties. Usage of trade is a regularly observed practice proved as a fact. Examine the parties’ trade or awareness and the place of performance.

topics.heading: Interpretation, waiver, and modification
topics.body: Repeated performance can show what an agreement has meant from the start, or show that a party gave up or changed a right under an express term. Under UCC § 1-303(f), even inconsistent conduct can support waiver or modification. A waiver affecting future performance can ordinarily be retracted by reasonable notice unless reliance would make retraction unjust.

topics.heading: Frigaliment and Hurst on specialized meaning
topics.body: Frigaliment tested the disputed meaning of chicken against incorporated government standards, market price, communications, and evidence of trade practice. The buyer failed to establish its narrower reading. Hurst allowed evidence that the trade rounded protein measurements even though the percentage in the written specification appeared exact.

topics.heading: Apply each party’s knowledge at formation
topics.body: Restatement §§ 20 and 201 ask who knew or had reason to know of the competing meaning. A party less aware of the mismatch can prevail when the other had the corresponding knowledge. Materially different readings can defeat mutual assent when neither party knew or should have known of the other’s meaning, or when both did.

topics.heading: When trade practice qualifies price, quantity, or remedies
topics.body: Nanakuli allowed evidence of price protection and the parties’ performance to support a limited qualification of posted prices. Columbia Nitrogen allowed evidence about flexibility in price and quantity despite a detailed writing. Figgie used proof of a trade practice to supply an exclusive remedy, and the refund fulfilled that remedy.

topics.heading: Drafting around commercial practices
topics.body: Davis compares a targeted no-waiver provision with an express exclusion of course of performance, course of dealing, and usage of trade. Ask what a merger clause excludes and whether the parties carefully negated the specific practice asserted. The policy tradeoff is between predictable written terms and the cost of specifying every shared convention.

conflicts.heading: Plain meaning depends on the governing approach
conflicts.body: Slide 4 puts explanation of unambiguous language in its exclusion list, then separately permits commercial context to establish meaning. Slides 19–20 show the UCC distinction. Treat the exclusion as a feature of a restrictive interpretive approach. Commercial context under §§ 1-303 and 2-202 does not require an ambiguity found from the writing alone.

title: Good faith in performance

topics.heading: Good faith constrains performance and enforcement
topics.body: UCC §§ 1-304 and 1-302(b) impose good faith and permit an agreement to set standards that are not manifestly unreasonable. The model definition combines honesty and reasonable commercial standards. Restatement § 205 connects performance and enforcement to the agreed purpose and the parties’ justified expectations.

topics.heading: Use the obligation the parties created
topics.body: Good faith is especially useful when a party can control quantity, satisfaction of a condition, or royalty-generating distribution. Begin with the bargain and the discretion it leaves. The slides distinguish this inquiry from fiduciary loyalty, tort liability, and a separate best-efforts promise.

topics.heading: Dalton and promised consideration of evidence
topics.body: ETS’s promise to accept relevant information required meaningful consideration and a nonarbitrary decision. The New York Court of Appeals did not require ETS to investigate externally or validate the score. It ordered reconsideration under the promised process. Slide 12 compares that implication with later SAT language that expressly requires considering submissions.

topics.heading: Market Street and opportunistic performance
topics.body: Under a lease financing clause, failed negotiations could trigger a valuable purchase option. Posner asked whether the tenant deliberately induced or exploited the pension trust’s oversight. The court remanded because intent remained disputed. The drafting hypotheticals compare an unconditional option, an express notice condition, and a rule keyed to trickery.

topics.heading: Bloor and the evidence of best efforts
topics.body: Falstaff promised best efforts to promote Ballantine sales and owed a royalty tied to volume. The sales graph compares Ballantine’s steep decline with Falstaff and other brewers. The court looked at the distribution decisions and manageable steps Falstaff could have considered while allowing it to protect its own financial viability.

topics.heading: Northwest and federal preemption
topics.body: The Airline Deregulation Act displaced Ginsberg’s Minnesota implied-covenant claim because the state imposed the obligation and the claim related to airline rates or services. Identify any independently enforceable promise the airline actually undertook. The distinction matters where a frequent-flyer program gives the airline broad discretion.

topics.heading: Compare the Commonwealth authorities
topics.body: Ng Giap Hon rejected a general implied duty under Singapore law. The assigned comparative notes use English and Canadian authorities to test narrower controls on contractual discretion and dishonest performance. Identify the particular jurisdiction, duty, and contract power when drawing comparisons.

conflicts.heading: The Dalton cancellation clause is reversed on slide 11
conflicts.body: The written bulletin gave ETS a right to cancel a score when it had reason to question validity, subject to the promised process. The slide’s phrase “right to refuse to cancel” reverses the reservation. The casebook at p. 720 and 87 N.Y.2d at 387 supply the correct clause.

title: Standard form contracts

topics.heading: Standardization, consent, and the informed minority
topics.body: Standard forms save negotiation and drafting costs, while limited choice and low attention can weaken the market’s discipline. Davis pairs a software study finding almost nobody opened the license with a separate study finding that later-delivered software terms were no worse by its measure. Each study answers a different question in a particular market.

topics.heading: Late terms require notice and a practical opportunity to exit
topics.body: RLCC § 2(b) asks what the customer was told before committing, whether the customer could review the late term, and whether the customer could end the transaction afterward without unreasonable cost, loss of value, or burden. The business must establish these facts. Apply that framework separately from the governing law in Carnival.

topics.heading: Consumer assurances and the parol-evidence rule
topics.body: RLCC §§ 8 and 9 protect qualifying precontract factual assurances and promises. A boilerplate term may fail to limit the resulting obligation, and an inconsistent term may fail to constitute a final expression on that subject. Identify the business’s specific assurance and the standard term invoked against it.

topics.heading: Reasonable expectations and standardized assent
topics.body: Restatement § 211 generally recognizes assent to the standard writing and favors treating similarly situated parties alike. A term drops out where the drafter had reason to believe the customer would withhold assent if aware of it. Consider negotiations, conspicuous language, commercial context, and an unusual or oppressive provision.

topics.heading: Graham and Carnival test different controls
topics.body: Graham treats even a sophisticated concert promoter as an adherent where the union form was effectively unavoidable. Industry expectations supported arbitration, while the union’s control over the arbitrator made the term unenforceable. Carnival reviews a cruise-ticket forum clause for fundamental fairness and treats notice as conceded on its record.

topics.heading: Statutory policing in the United States and Europe
topics.body: Doe illustrates how a dating-services statute can mandate disclosures, cancellation rights, and other minimum protections. The EU directive pairs understandable drafting with review of significant imbalance in standard terms. Compare these rules with case-by-case assent, expectations, and fairness review.

topics.heading: Contract remedies when a mandatory duty is preempted
topics.body: The class opens by revisiting Ginsberg. Identify express obligations a customer could still invoke when federal law preempts a state-imposed implied covenant. Evaluate those obligations alongside the terms prescribing the airline’s own exercise of discretion.

conflicts.heading: Carnival did not decide when the Shutes assented
conflicts.body: Slides 16–17 invite applying the later-term notice framework as a classroom hypothetical. The Supreme Court’s majority treated notice as conceded and had no occasion to decide adequacy of notice. The dissent discussed receipt after payment and the practical ability to cancel. The July 2019 and 2021 market-share graph is a later comparator.

conflicts.heading: The EU annex identifies candidates for review
conflicts.body: Slide 19’s reference to arbitration is shorthand. Directive 93/13/EEC, Article 3 and Annex 1(q), identify terms that impede legal remedies, including certain compulsory arbitration provisions, as potentially unfair. The annex is indicative and requires assessment under the directive and relevant implementing law.

title: Unconscionability

topics.heading: Test choice and the substance of the bargain
topics.body: Williams asks about meaningful choice and terms unreasonably favorable to the other side. Consider the opportunity to understand the terms, relative bargaining power and realistically available alternatives. Evaluate substantive harshness in light of the transaction and commercial setting.

topics.heading: Williams and cross-collateral repossession
topics.body: Installment payments were spread across outstanding purchases, leaving each item subject to repossession until the total balance was paid. The majority recognized unconscionability review and remanded for findings. The dissent emphasized apparent knowledge and possible effects on access to credit.

topics.heading: Stoll and an oppressive additional term
topics.body: After agreeing to a substantial price for the real estate, the buyers purportedly gave the seller rights to poultry litter for thirty years. Test procedural unfairness through the buyers’ ability to understand the clause, and substantive unfairness through its economic value and duration.

topics.heading: Choose the remedy after finding unconscionability
topics.body: UCC § 2-302 and Restatement § 208 allow refusing enforcement, enforcing the remainder without the term, or limiting the term to avoid an unconscionable result. Davis considers several replacement rules and asks how each allocation affects incentives to draft aggressive terms.

topics.heading: Compare ex ante statutory protection
topics.body: The EU directive uses transparency and substantive unfairness controls. Doe illustrates targeted mandatory protections such as a cooling-off period and required disclosures. Compare the difficulty of proving unfairness case by case with the costs and benefits of setting the obligation in advance.

topics.heading: Anderson separates amendment, temporal scope, and fairness
topics.body: Evaluate whether Binance gave adequate notice of the arbitration amendment, whether its terms reached existing disputes, and whether the heading actually waived class proceedings in court. The assigned 2026 order rejected arbitration and the purported waiver for the remaining pre-amendment claims. The RLCC and EU questions are comparative applications.

conflicts.heading: The four replacement options are classroom alternatives
conflicts.body: Slide 11 presents alternative ways to respond to an unconscionable term. UCC § 2-302 and Restatement § 208 expressly authorize refusal, severance, and limiting application to avoid an unconscionable result. The slide’s least-favorable substitution is a policy option and requires independent support under the governing law.

conflicts.heading: An arbitration clause is not categorically on an EU blacklist
conflicts.body: Slide 13 pairs arbitration with the indicative EU annex. Article 3 and Annex 1(q) call for assessing whether the clause hinders legal remedies. Individual jurisdictions may impose stronger rules. Anderson itself concerns notice, amendment scope, and ambiguous drafting under U.S. law.

title: Public policy

topics.heading: Tie unenforceability to a specific policy
topics.body: Identify a statute or recognized policy and how the bargain implicates it. The connection differs when performance itself is unlawful, an otherwise lawful bargain was procured unlawfully, or performance of a lawful promise facilitates another party’s wrongful conduct.

topics.heading: Distinguish enforcement, severance, restitution, and equitable relief
topics.body: Compare the interests supporting enforcement with the strength of the policy, the relationship between the misconduct and the bargain, and the risk of forfeiture. Then consider severance and restitution independently. Relative culpability and unclean hands can affect the availability of particular remedies.

topics.heading: Blossom Farm and X.L.O. Concrete mark different links to illegality
topics.body: Blossom Farm involved a seller knowingly helping the buyer’s continuing mislabeling scheme. X.L.O. Concrete required a developed record on whether payment for construction would enforce the anticompetitive arrangement itself. The extent of the connection matters to deterrence and the risk of a forfeiture unrelated to the policy.

topics.heading: Bribery and transnational public policy
topics.body: In World Duty Free v. Kenya, the arbitral tribunal refused to enforce a concession procured by bribing the head of state. Davis asks how the tribunal identified transnational public policy, what weight a claimed local custom could have, and how denying enforcement affects incentives for firms and states.

topics.heading: Noncompetes and the rule of reason
topics.body: Analyze the underlying transaction, legitimate interests, and the restriction’s duration, geographic reach, and activities covered. Account for hardship to the worker and harm to the public. The slides compare employee, business-sale, and partnership covenants, then use survey evidence and examples to examine effects on competition and information sharing.

topics.heading: Hassler and the refusal to rewrite
topics.body: The Wyoming Supreme Court declined to reshape a covenant with unreasonable time and geographic limits despite a clause asking the court to substitute the maximum permissible restraint. The example exposes the incentive to draft broadly if courts routinely rescue overreaching terms.

topics.heading: Federal rule removal and state-law variation
topics.body: The FTC removed its Non-Compete Rule from the Code of Federal Regulations effective February 12, 2026 following judicial vacatur. Davis compares California’s general prohibition with Massachusetts’s qualified notice, consideration, duration, and other requirements. Verify the governing jurisdiction and agreement date before applying either model.

conflicts.heading: Hardship and public injury are not cumulative requirements
conflicts.body: Slide 15’s list can be read to require excessive scope, undue hardship, and public injury together. Restatement § 188 instead treats a restraint as unreasonable if it is greater than needed to protect a legitimate interest, or if the promisee’s need is outweighed by the hardship to the promisor and likely public injury. Governing statutes can replace the common-law test.

conflicts.heading: Massachusetts uses business-day notice and a qualified duration cap
conflicts.body: Slide 18’s 10-day and 12-month bullets compress Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 149, § 24L(b)(i)–(iv). Notice periods use business days. Mid-employment agreements require independent fair consideration, and the duration can reach two years for specified breaches of fiduciary duty or unlawful taking of employer property.

conflicts.heading: Wyoming later changed the statutory baseline
conflicts.body: Hassler remains the assigned 2022 decision. For contracts entered into on or after July 1, 2025, Wyo. Stat. § 1-23-108 generally voids covered labor noncompetes, subject to its enumerated exceptions. 2025 Wyoming Session Laws ch. 170 preserves contracts entered into before that date from the new act.

title: Express and constructive conditions

topics.heading: An event can be a duty, a condition or a timing marker
topics.body: Ask whether the event is promised, whether another duty depends on its occurrence and whether the language merely fixes when payment comes due. The shipping exercise can be drafted as a promise to sail with the next wind, as a trigger for a premium, or as both. Peacock treated the ambiguous payment clause as determining reasonable timing and required clear language to shift the owner’s credit risk to subcontractors.

topics.heading: The precise financing condition matters
topics.body: Luttinger compares the loan the parties specified with the more expensive financing the buyers could actually obtain. The seller’s offer to subsidize the difference did not turn that loan into a qualifying commitment. Analyze due diligence separately from whether the condition occurred and ask whose protection the condition serves in the cash-purchase hypothetical.

topics.heading: Waiver, prevention and forfeiture
topics.body: Separate an advance waiver, an election to go forward after failure, and an agreed modification. Material contribution to nonoccurrence through breach can excuse a condition under § 245. Section 229 permits a limited excuse for disproportionate forfeiture when occurrence was not a material part of the exchange.

topics.heading: Satisfaction and good faith
topics.body: Mattei distinguishes objective reasonableness for commercial value or functional fitness from honest subjective dissatisfaction for matters of judgment or taste. The class also asks how an architect’s certification changes the problem. Identify whose satisfaction the contract requires and the standard that governs it.

topics.heading: Constructive conditions and materiality
topics.body: An uncured material failure can excuse the other side’s remaining performance. In Kingston, security for the purchase price had to precede transfer of the business. In Jacob & Youngs, the equivalence of the substituted pipe, the purpose of the specification and the waste of replacing it matter to substantial performance. A monetary allowance for breach remains a separate question.

topics.heading: Dividing performance into agreed equivalents
topics.body: Restatement § 240 asks whether part performances can be paired as agreed equivalents. Gill allowed recovery for logs actually delivered under a unit-price arrangement. The halfway-delivery question tests whether a court can invent a new unit of payment when the parties paired payment with completed delivery.

topics.heading: Net benefit after material breach
topics.body: Nelson tests restitution for the party whose failure prevented recovery of the contract balance. Measure the benefit retained and account for the owner’s payments and losses from the breach. The policy tradeoff is avoiding a windfall while preserving the owner’s protection against defective work.

conflicts.heading: Article 2 rejection and cure
conflicts.body: The slide’s reference to any breach is shorthand for the ordinary perfect-tender rule governing an initial tender. Section 2-601 is subject to agreed limits and installment-contract rules. Account for timely rejection, applicable cure and the distinct rules after acceptance. The deck identifies perfect tender as outside the lecture’s main coverage.

title: Mistake, impracticability and frustration

topics.heading: Mistake about meaning and mistake about facts
topics.body: The Peerless hypothetical tests whether materially different meanings prevent assent under § 20. Mistake under §§ 152–154 instead concerns a basic assumption about existing facts. Determine whether the error was mutual or unilateral and, for unilateral mistake, test unconscionability or the other party’s knowledge or fault.

topics.heading: Allocate risk before deciding excuse
topics.body: Risk can follow the parties’ agreement, conscious reliance on limited knowledge or a court’s reasonable allocation. Paradine and Stees illustrate strict enforcement of undertaken duties. The class compares that baseline with presumed intent, fairness and the relative ability to prevent, insure against or absorb the loss.

topics.heading: Renner and the remedy after avoidance
topics.body: The parties shared a material mistake about water availability for jojoba cultivation. Rescission opens an accounting for each side’s transfers or benefits. The buyers’ expenditures on the land matter to restitution to the extent they benefited the sellers. This accounting differs from awarding the profit of the hoped-for venture.

topics.heading: Impracticability and the particular means of performance
topics.body: Taylor treats accidental loss of the particular music hall as defeating a basic assumption. Transatlantic tests whether a costlier available route is impracticable. The shipping-risk diagram traces the same loss from higher overall costs to fuel usage, canal closure and its possible causes, showing why how narrowly the risk is framed affects the analysis.

topics.heading: Frustration and the parties’ shared purpose
topics.body: In Krell, the cancellation of the coronation procession defeated the shared foundation of hiring the viewing rooms even though the rooms could be supplied. The taxi comparison asks when a customer’s purpose becomes a basic assumption of the exchange. The pandemic scenario tests whether a different event and contract change the result.

topics.heading: Force majeure turns on the clause’s scope
topics.body: Compare the example covering delays outside a party’s reasonable control with the lease clause permitting temporary excuse but expressly preserving most rent obligations and excluding financing shortfalls. Identify the event, causal link, obligation covered, duration and contractual exceptions before reaching default excuse doctrine.

conflicts.heading: Adjustment after excuse and reformation of a writing
conflicts.body: Slide 11 groups several forms of equitable relief under reformation. Distinguish restitution after avoidance, equitable adjustment after supervening events and reformation of a writing that fails to express the agreement. A material mistake or later event does not automatically authorize a court to rewrite contract terms.

title: Overview of remedies and specific relief

topics.heading: Identify the remedial baseline
topics.body: Expectation asks where performance would have left the promisee. Reliance asks where the promisee would have been without the agreement. Restitution looks to benefits transferred. The lecture also compares possible gain-based, stipulated and punitive remedies as policy alternatives, with their own legal limits.

topics.heading: Adequacy of damages and the equitable inquiry
topics.body: Consider realistic substitute performance, valuation and practical enforceability. The deck treats land as traditionally presumptively unique and uses UCC § 2-716’s uniqueness or other proper circumstances standard for goods. Equitable considerations include delay, fairness and supervision. The CISG discussion adds Article 28’s forum-law qualification.

topics.heading: Personal services and negative injunctions
topics.body: The class tests supervision, hardship and compelled-service concerns where a contract calls for skill and discretion. A negative covenant concerning especially distinctive services can raise a different equitable question. Consider what the requested injunction would require the promisor to do in practice.

topics.heading: Klein and Walgreen on substitute relief
topics.body: Compare an aircraft sale, where comparable replacements and monetary damages were available, with a lease exclusivity clause whose breach would make a decade of competitive losses difficult to estimate. Walgreen compares the cost of measuring damages with the cost of enforcing an injunction and bargaining after it issues.

topics.heading: Same machine allocation, different surplus
topics.body: The worked diagrams send the machine to buyer C under three arrangements. Expectation damages leave the original buyer with $400 and the seller with $500. With specific performance and costless resale or renegotiation at the stated prices, the original buyer receives $600 in surplus and the seller receives $300. The possibility of transfer and the distribution of gains are distinct questions.

topics.heading: The limits of efficient breach
topics.body: Expectation damages create the model’s incentive only when actors have suitable information about losses. Bargaining costs, obstacles to resale, reliance incentives and judicial error can change outcomes. The deck treats the preference for expectation damages as a policy hypothesis to test.

topics.heading: Cosby and reliance on a government assurance
topics.body: The lecture tests promise, authority, reliance and remedy using § 90 as a framework for discussion. The court’s actual ground was fundamental fairness after a nonprosecution assurance induced surrender of the privilege against self-incrimination. The remedy enforced the assurance by barring retrial.

file: Class 23_Losing contracts_Cost vs value of performance - Copy (1).pptx
title: Losing contracts and the cost or value of performance

topics.heading: Price the performance baseline
topics.body: The surgery table contrasts the position without the agreement, the position with promised performance and the actual result. For expectation, start with the lost value of what was promised, subtract costs or losses avoided, and add other recoverable losses such as corrective treatment where supported. The table is a classroom hypothetical drawn loosely from Sullivan.

topics.heading: Algernon Blair and the loss-making bargain
topics.body: A subcontractor that stopped after a material breach could seek the reasonable value of the labor and equipment supplied. The class compares that result with expectation on an unprofitable subcontract and asks how it affects a prime contractor’s incentive to substitute a cheaper performer.

topics.heading: Completion cost, market diminution and personal value
topics.body: Each measure asks a different question. Section 348(2) provides alternatives when the injured party’s value loss from defective or unfinished construction cannot be proved with sufficient certainty. Reasonable completion cost is subject to the limit that it not be clearly disproportionate to the probable loss in value to the injured party.

topics.heading: Plante and the misplaced wall
topics.body: Substantial performance let the builder recover the balance subject to deductions. Correcting a wall that caused no demonstrated market loss would require disproportionate work. The deck asks whether either completion cost or market price captures what the promisee personally lost.

topics.heading: Groves, Peevyhouse and the value of restoration
topics.body: Groves allowed a completion-cost measure for deliberate nonperformance of the restoration promise. Peevyhouse limited recovery to market diminution after treating restoration as incidental and its cost as grossly disproportionate. The lecture asks how price, willingness to pay and the parties’ bargaining choices bear on the importance of restoration.

topics.heading: Drafting the restoration bargain
topics.body: The Weevyhouses exercise asks how to make restoration central and protect the landowners before signing. Compare how express restoration milestones, payment security and a defensible agreed remedy address the risk, then analyze completion cost and market diminution if the language is left unchanged.

title: Limitations on damages

topics.heading: Alternative purposes of default rules
topics.body: A majoritarian default saves the cost of writing a term many parties want. A penalty default can instead prompt the party with better information to disclose it. The lecture applies that distinction to the incentives created by damages limits, including disclosure, precautions, insurance and agreed damages.

topics.heading: Avoidable loss after a clear breach or repudiation
topics.body: Rockingham limits recovery for expenditures the builder incurred after receiving an unequivocal repudiation. The hypothetical separates suspected cancellation from a clear repudiation and asks how to handle reasonable but unsuccessful efforts to find substitute work. Section 350 accounts for risk, burden, expense and humiliation.

topics.heading: Comparable substitute work
topics.body: Parker compares the promised musical role with a substitute western. The majority treated significantly different or inferior work as outside the required mitigation inquiry. The dissent wanted factual evaluation of comparability. The drafted-payment hypothetical asks whether express guaranteed compensation can change the allocation.

topics.heading: Foreseeability at contract formation
topics.body: Hadley asks whether the loss follows in the ordinary course or from special circumstances the parties had reason to contemplate when they contracted. The discussion tests when a shipping customer must disclose unusual stakes and why learning them only after formation ordinarily does not supply the necessary contemporaneous notice.

topics.heading: Restatement, CISG and Article 2 formulations
topics.body: The lecture compares Hadley and § 351 with CISG Article 74’s foresight of a possible consequence and UCC § 2-715’s buyer-side consequential-loss inquiry. In Article 2, assess requirements the seller had reason to know and whether cover or another reasonable step could prevent loss. Analyze consequential loss and available market or cover measures separately.

topics.heading: Kenford and assumption of extraordinary loss
topics.body: The county could anticipate that a stadium would affect nearby land values without undertaking liability for lost appreciation. The lecture distinguishes that reasoning from ordinary foreseeability and asks how explicit allocations or damage exclusions could change the result. The Atlas notes that UCC § 2-715 rejects the tacit-agreement test.

topics.heading: Proof of uncertain profits and lost opportunities
topics.body: Fera asks whether evidence permits a reasonable estimate of the new business’s lost profits. The lecture tests how operating history, comparable stores and disagreement among experts change the proof. The quiz-finalist example compares denial, full-value recovery and probability-weighted recovery as competing approaches to a lost chance.
